author: Kortney Grimm
title: "It gave me a second life": Local man able to get LVAD defunctionalized after his heart regained enough strength - NewsBreak
text:
By Kortney Grimm ,
1 hours ago
FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WANE) — It all started in 2023 when Mitchell Evenson was being treated for GI issues. After being sedated for a scope due to those issues, he went into total heart failure.
Doctors quickly performed CPR, and Evenson spent the next five days in an induced coma.
He was then moved to Lutheran Hospital, where the heart failure team took over, trying to figure out what happened to Evenson.
“They figured out that I had 5% of my heart working,” he said. “The left side of my heart was not working at all, and the right side was trying to take over everything.”
That hospital stay turned into 63 days in total, and Evenson went home with a Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD), a mechanical pump that is implanted into heart failure patients.
“It’s life-saving therapies,” Dr. Asim Mohammed, Advanced Heart Failure Cardiologist at Lutheran Health, said. “It’s standard care if you have end-stage heart failure, meaning your heart is just giving out. Without providing this kind of support, either with the LVAD or transplant, your days are limited.”
Evenson spent the next two years with the LVAD, believing this would be his everyday life for the rest of his life.
Over those two years of check-ups and ultrasounds, doctors found that his heart was actually recovering and getting stronger due to the LVAD. Recently, in November, doctors said that they could defunctionalize his LVAD because of all the progress.
“He said I was up above the 55%, what it needed to be at,” Evenson said. “So, we went from there, and it was a new day for me.”
Evenson and his doctors then completed the procedure later in November.
“In a small fraction of patients, the heart function does come back where we feel confident enough to really defunctionalize the LVAD,” Mohammed said. “Meaning we don’t physically take the heart pump out, but we just turn it off and let the heart take over the heart function.”
Mohammed added that they are now adding a few decades onto the lives of patients instead of a few months with the technology that the LVAD brings.
“That’s the beauty of the device, it’s just not keeping them alive, but they’re actually living,” Mohammed said. “Present for their family and their children, so that’s what gives me the immense joy.”
This is a very rare situation, as Lutheran Hospital says this procedure has been done less than 10 times in the hospital’s history.
“It gave me a second life,” Evenson said. “Knowing the fact that my heart is still my heart, and it’s strong enough to go on with my family.”
